# Updated by AirvZxf {#appendix-j.-updated-by-airvzxf}

I\'m [Israel Roldan][AJ-IsraelRoldan]. I wanted to learn the GNU Assembler (`as` or `gas`), and I didn\'t find many resources, but this book is great.

This is the x86-64 edition of the book, for 64-bit programs. It started
from the [x86 32-bit edition][AJ-X86-32Edition], which is maintained in
its own repository, but it was rewritten as a new book: it teaches how
64-bit Linux programs are written today, compares them with Rust and
Python, and never needs the 32-bit material.

All the information is in my [GitHub repository][AJ-MyGitHubRepository]. To check the progress of this project and the pending reviews go to the [TO-DO\'s][AJ-MyTodoList] list. The scripts `make.bash` and `test.bash` assemble, link and test every one of the [example programs][AJ-AsmSourceCode], including the solutions of Appendix K, and the build checks that they follow the rules of the book: a non-executable stack and no absolute addresses.

Motivations {#motivations}
-----------

- I believe that Linux is the future. I dream of a world where everyone uses Linux on their laptops and desktop computers, and all the video game companies make perfect games for Linux.

- I was researching the GNU Assembler (“as” or “gas”), but unfortunately there are not many resources: most of them talk about the most popular assemblers, “[NASM][AJ-NASM]” and “[FASM][AJ-FASM]”.

- Why NOT focus on “NASM” or “FASM”? I started with “NASM”, and in 2020 I thought that its active development had stopped. I was wrong: NASM is still maintained (version 3.02 came out in June 2026). I researched “FASM”, and it looks awesome, but then I discovered a curious detail. These assemblers can build programs for many architectures, which is powerful, but to be that compatible they spend a lot of effort to create the most generic binary possible ([^AJ-1]). At that moment I started to consider using the native Linux assembler, because for me the idea of a multi-architecture assembler is mostly marketing. I have been a software developer for over 20 years (since 2005), and I have never created a multi-architecture system, not even in my personal projects. Why would I live in a utopia and want a tool that converts my programs to other architectures, if I always create programs for Linux and very rarely for Windows? In those cases I usually use Python or Java. Note: this is my personal point of view.

- Why use assembly rather than other languages? In some cases, assembly is faster than C. Around 2020, I wrote [benchmarks][AJ-MyBenchmarks] that compute Fibonacci numbers, and compared my assembly solutions, examples that I found on the Internet, and a C version: without `printf`, the assembly programs ran in about 0.5 seconds and the C program in about 0.8 seconds, but with `printf` they all ran at the same speed. See also the [C benchmarks][AJ-CBenchmarks]. [Chapter 11](11-high-level-languages.qmd#what-the-compiler-generates) and [Chapter 12](12-optimization.qmd#chapter-12-optimization) show how much a modern optimizing compiler does on its own.

- Why update this book? This book is one of the best that I found, but it has many areas of opportunity. I read up to Chapter 3 and had three doubts about the final exercises, but there were no answers. The book said that we had seen the subject, and I reviewed all the chapters, and we hadn't.

- Deep thanks to the men and companies who inspired me to be better and thanks to the Open Source: [Linus Torvalds][AJ-LinusTorvalds], [Richard Stallman][AJ-RichardStallman], [Linux][AJ-Linux], [GNU][AJ-GNU], [GitHub][AJ-GitHub].

[^AJ-1]: [FASM: Design Principles, or Why FASM Is Different][AJ-FasmDesignPrinciples] sections “4) Resolving The Code” and “5) Complex Solutions With Simple Features”. In general, this document provides an overview of the complexity behind a multi-architecture assembler.
